newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Japan's Hashimoto arrives in Hanoi to warm welcome.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto arrives in Hanoi to warm welcome.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto arrived in Vietnam on Saturday on the fourth leg of a five-nation tour of Southeast Asia that has been overshadowed by the hostage crisis in Peru.

The two countries' national flags fluttered side-by-side in the sunshine at Hanoi's Noi Bai airport as high-ranking officials came forward to greet the state leader of their country's biggest aid donor and main trading partner.

The latest leg of Hashimoto's trip began after Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's government renewed talks late on Friday with Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
The talks aim to negotiate a peaceful solution to the 24-day-old crisis.

Hashimoto is due to be received by Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet at the Presidential Palace, where he will sign aid pledges worth more than $760 million, and then meet Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi.
He will visit the mausoleum of communist Vietnam's revered founding father, Ho Chi Minh, and a Japanese school on Sunday before leaving for his tour's last stop, Singapore.
The Japanese leader -- who marked his first anniversary in office on Saturday -- is expected to give a key address on Tokyo's Asia-Pacific policy in Singapore on Tuesday.

Japan's ambassador to Hanoi, Katsunari Suzuki, told the official Vietnam News Agency that Hashimoto would reaffirm his support for the communist party's decade-old drive for reform along market lines.
"Japan will continue to support Vietnam's ongoing renovation policy..." he said. "The two leaders will also examine measures to promote the relationship between Japan and ASEAN in the 21st century."

The Communist Party's official daily, Nhan Dan, said in an editorial that the two countries were determined to broaden a relationship which in recent years has hinged on Japan's development aid and direct investment.
Now, with Vietnam a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and Japan keen to boost ties with the seven-nation grouping, ties are likely to be closer.

Many older Vietnamese remember Japan's World War Two occupation of their country, which has been blamed for a devastating famine from 1943 to 1945. But that era is rarely mentioned by politicians from either country these days.
Japan is the leading donor of official development aid (ODA) to Vietnam, pledging $3.23 billion between 1992 and 1996.

It is also Vietnam's biggest bilateral trading partner. Some $3.0 billion worth of goods and services were traded between the two countries last year, accounting for about one-sixth of Vietnam's combined import and export volume.
Hanoi's 1995 trade surplus with Japan was about $750 million.
Japanese companies have earmarked some $2.7 billion for investment projects, placing their nation second in a growing list of countries looking for a share in Vietnam's economic boom.
